deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio [23v] carries a German poem of three four-line stanzas in rhymed couplets (aabb). The metre is mostly amphibrachic or anapaestic, with four stresses per line.

Content of the stanzas:
- Stanza 1: a lament ('Komm Hoffnung und wehe mir Tröstungen zu; / Das Herz ist gebrochen, dahin ist die Ruh ...').
- Stanza 2: an appeal to the breeze to carry tears of sorrow to the faithless youth ('dem Jünglinge'). It ends with the quoted message: 'Du siehst sie nicht wieder, sie tödtet der Schmerz.'
- Stanza 3: longing for the grave as the place of peace ('Im Grabe ists stille ... dort lohnet die Palme ein liebendes Herz').

Other marks:
- A calligraphic flourish (paraph) at the lower right.
- A pencil numeral '4' at the upper right, probably a later archival or foliation mark.
- A trace of another letter below the last line at the bottom edge.

The theme and diction resemble sentimental lyric of the 1790s–1800s, the 'Mädchens Klage' type. Phrases such as 'dahin ist die Ruh' echo Goethe's 'Meine Ruh ist hin' and Schiller's 'Des Mädchens Klage'. I cannot securely identify the source text or its author.

The hand is a fairly rounded, schoolish German Kurrent. It is not obviously Gauss's mathematical hand, so the poem may be a copy by Gauss or by someone else, with the sheet later reused. The sheet seems to have been reused for mathematics: the adjacent pages (23r and the next leaf, numbered 23/24) hold Latin number-theoretic material. That material covers divisibility of polynomials modulo p^m, and a gcd expressed as a linear combination k·λ + γ·C = λ'. Nothing on this side connects to that mathematics.

results.what: Copy of a sentimental German poem (three stanzas, rhymed couplets) on a leaf otherwise used for number-theoretic notes
results.usually_credited_to: unidentified poet; resembles late-18th-century German sentimental lyric

deep.surprise_reason: The page has no mathematical content. A copied poem on a reused sheet in a mathematical bundle is unremarkable. The only point of interest is biographical or archival: who wrote out the poem, and whether the hand is Gauss's.
transcription_corrections: Line 7: the word read as "lispl'[?]" appears to be "lisple" (imperative of 'lispeln'), i.e. 'Und lisple ihm traulich ins treulose Herz'.
Line 1: 'wehe' (imperative of 'wehen') is consistent with the image; 'Tröstungen' is confirmed.
Line 6: 'Weh' is likewise the imperative of 'wehen' ('Weh Thränen der Wehmuth dem Jünglinge zu'), not the interjection.
The machine transcription omits the pencil '4' at the upper right, the calligraphic flourish (paraph) at the lower right, and a partial letter at the bottom edge below the last line.
Line 9: the manuscript has 'Im Grabe ists stille' (contracted 'ists', no apostrophe), as transcribed; line-initial capitalisation in stanza 3 ('dort') is lowercase in the original, as transcribed.
